articles.headline: Nominating Convention.
articles.text: A convention of the citizens and qualified voters of Billings county, will be held Monday evening, March 1, 1886, to place in nomination a list of county officers to be voted for on the second Monday in April, 1886 and to hold office until the next regular fall election. A full attendance is requested.
articles.summary: Call for a Billings County nominating convention on March 1, 1886, to name candidates for the April county election.

articles.text: It seems that we are on the eve of one of the greatest railroad wars the United States has ever known. Through rates from Chicago to San Francisco have been reduced to $30, first class and $20, second class. All the Pacific roads have been interested except the Canadian Pacific. Now, by a combination with the Manitoba, they will begin on June 15, to run through trains from St. Paul via the Manitoba and Canadian Pacific to the Pacific terminus of the latter. This will make an important factor in the fight and we very much doubt if any of the Pacific roads make money this summer.
articles.summary: Editorial note on a coming transcontinental rate war, with Chicago-San Francisco fares cut to $30 and $20.

articles.text:
There is at least one poliiician who dares state what he knows to be the facts concerning the hypocrisy over civil service reform. Witness the following from Robert G. Ingersoll:

"If the president feels that he is bound to carry out the civil service law, ought not the senate to feel the same way? Is it not the duty of the senate to see to it that the president does not, with its advice and consent, violate the civil service law? Is the consent of the senate a mere matter of form? In these appointments the president is not independent of or above the senate; they are equal, and each has the right to 'honor bright' with the other, at least. As long as the foolish law is unrepealed it must be carried out. Neither party is in favor of civil service reform, and never was. The republican party did not carry it out, and did not intend to. The president has the right to nominate. Under the law as it is now, when the president wants to appoint a clerk, or when one of his secretaries wants one, four names are sent, and from these four names the choice has to be made. This is clearly an invasion of the rights of the executive. If they have the right to compel the president to choose from four, why not from three, or two? Why not name the one, and have done with it? The law is worse than unconstitutional, it is absurd".—[Col. Ingersoll.
articles.summary: Editorial quoting Robert G. Ingersoll attacking civil service reform as hypocrisy.

articles.text: The snow has almost entirely go only a few small drifts being left in sheltered spots. Almost all the creeks have running water, however, and no danger to cattle interests is apprehended unless everything is frozen up solid.
articles.summary: The snow is nearly gone and the creeks are running; no danger to cattle is expected unless a hard freeze comes.

articles.text: One of the best articles in the constitution of the National range association, is the one establishing a black-list, on which the names of all men in any way connected with the cattle business and who are known to be dishonest, shall be enrolled. These men are to be boycotted and thus driven out of the business. We confidently look for similar action to be taken at the coming meeting of the Montana association.
articles.summary: Packard praises the National range association's black-list of dishonest cattlemen and hopes the Montana association will follow.

articles.headline: Cheaper Beef.
articles.text: NEW YORK, Feb. 22.—The Marquis de Mores has not yet started for his cattle ranch in the west. He has been delayed here to perfect a scheme which will probably have considerable effect on the price of meats in this city. A Tribune reporter met him incidentally up town last night and although the project is not yet fully ripe, he explained the principal features of it. "We propose" he said, "to stop the expense of middlemen and send meats direct from the producer to the consumer. I have discovered that in the practical working of the cattle business as at present conducted, there are eleven middlemen, each of whom must have a profit before the meat reaches the consumer. The wholesalers are eating us up. We propose to start retail shops in all the tenement-house districts of the city, where our meats will be sold on account of the company. The cattle will be killed at our abattoir. The beef will be shipped in refrigerator crrs. It will be delivered to a central market, and from there distributed to the different shops. We shall have the scheme at work in about sixty days. The details are now being perfected. The advantage to the consumer will amount to from 2 to 4 cents per pound all around. We think we might as well give the consumer the benefit of this profit which now goes to the middlemen."
articles.summary: New York dispatch of Feb. 22 reporting that the Marquis de Morès, delayed in New York, outlined a plan to sell his beef directly through company retail shops in the city.

articles.text: Range cattle, especially cows with sucking calves, are far from being in good condition. The small loss, almost nothing so far, is not by any means on account of the good condition of the animals, but because of the unusual mildness of the winter. Had there been as many cold snaps as there were last winter, the loss now would probably have reached five per cent. or more. The only danger of severe loss now is in a protracted cold snap, before another snowfall; a danger that we are happy to state is very remote.
articles.summary: Range cattle are in poor condition, but losses have been almost nothing because of the unusually mild winter.

articles.text: In their last year's shipments, Ferris & Merrifield brought in several Polled-Angus cattle. It is a pleasure to see them now, brought into sharp contrast with the other cattle by their plump condition. They are not only in good fix, but are rolling in fat. The position of the Cow Boy for two years past that the black doddies are by long odds the best range cattle, has been abundantly proven by experience.
articles.summary: Polled-Angus cattle brought in by Ferris & Merrifield last year are in fine, fat condition, vindicating the Cow Boy's view of the breed.

articles.text: This winter, more than ever before, has the necessity been shown, of keeping cattle back from the river and creek bottoms. Rides over the ranges disclose the facts that a large number of poor cattle stay constantly on creek bottoms, where their existence is a slow starvation, owing to the almost total lack of feed. In almost every instance, the weakest cattle are found here, and although we have not yet seen a dead animal on the range, we are much mistaken if there is no loss among them. Back from the creeks, cattle are found to be in far better condition, having for the most part, plenty of feed. Many places were also found where no cattle had been all winter and where there is plenty of feed for the cattle now on the creek bottoms. It would require considerable extra work and expense to keep them back, but a look at the cattle ought to convince anyone of the advisability of the plan.
articles.summary: Packard urges ranchmen to keep cattle back from the river and creek bottoms, where the weakest stock are starving for lack of feed.

articles.text: The river has gone down about eighteen inches in the last few days but is still too deep for fording. Beginning at the Ox-bow, for at least sixty miles up the river there is a solid jam of old ice, which is liable to do considerable damage when the thaw comes.
articles.summary: The Little Missouri has dropped eighteen inches but is still unfordable; an ice jam stretches sixty miles upriver from the Ox-bow.

articles.text: There are still a number of delinquent subscribers, whose subscriptions ran out last week and the week before. articles.text: The gang of midnight howlers who occasionally make night hideous, will be in condition to learn that a fine, costs and a trip to Dickinson come pretty high unless they stop their foolishness. It may be beyond the gang's comprehension, but there are people here who object to having the peace disturbed as it has been lately.
articles.summary: Warning to a gang of 'midnight howlers' disturbing the peace in Medora.

articles.text: The flood in the river has brought[?] out a plan by which horses at least, can be transferred from one side of the river to the other in perfect safety, during high water. The plan is to nail six inch boards on each side of the two boards already laid. Of course it would be better to take up the old boards and lay new two-inch plank. This would cost several hundred dollars as against about twenty-five for the first plan. There ought to be at least twenty-five men, interested enough to give a dollar each and thus insure the success of the plan.
articles.summary: Proposal to widen the existing river crossing so horses can cross safely at high water, funded by twenty-five dollar subscriptions.

articles.text: The advent of deputy sheriff Drury of Morton county and sheriff Sebastian of Stark county, last Sunday, caused a scattering among several bold and fearless youths, who, actuated by a lofty and heroic spirit, had saluted the departure of the train the night before, with the discharge of their six-shooters. It nearly scared a lady on the train to death, but of course this was not to be considered, in view of the glorious sport of frightening her into a fainting fit. Perhaps the officers had medals with which to reward the heroic daring of the six-shootists, but they didn't seem to think so and "several were the skips" when the officers were known to be in town.
articles.summary: Youths who fired six-shooters at a departing train scattered when two sheriffs arrived in Medora last Sunday.

articles.text: We have an over-stock of 3½ Studebaker wagons that the Studebaker M'f'g. Co. have instructed us to close out at $75 each. These wagons have never turned a wheel under a load, are new and first-class in every respect, have the Co's. full guarantee for 5,000 pounds, according to old freighters are the best-ironed and easiest running wagon of its size in the world, and cost at the factory, $[87?] in car lots. There never has and never will be such a bargain in wagons in this country. The $75 rate is cash of course and holds good for one or the lot of seven. The only reason for the cheap rate is to reduce stock on hand. For further particulars, call at or address the Cow Boy office.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy office offers seven 3½ Studebaker wagons at a $75 close-out price.

articles.headline: Notice of Election.
articles.text:
Notice is hereby given that on the Second (2nd.) Monday in April, 1886, at the following place, viz.: at the town of

Medora,

in the County of Billings, an election will be held for the following officers of said county of Billings, in said Territory of Dakota, in the organization of said county:

Three County Commissioners,
One Register of Deeds,
One County Clerk,
One Sheriff,
One Assessor,
One Judge of Probate,
One County Treasurer,
One County Surveyor,
One Coroner,
One Superintendent of Public Schools,
Four Justices of the Peace,
Four Constables,
and also for the temporary location of the
County seat of said county,
which election will be open at the hour of eight o'clock in the morning and will continue open until five o'clock in the afternoon of the same day.

Dated this 20th. day of January, 1886.

[Seal.] Gilbert A. Pierce, Governor.

M. L. McCormack, Secretary.
articles.summary: Governor Pierce's proclamation of the first Billings County election, to be held at Medora on the second Monday in April 1886, including the temporary county seat.
